issue: After Cotton, does a defect in a federal indictment deprive the court of jurisdiction, or does the Cotton rule apply only where the indictment charges some federal crime, leaving defects in an indictment that fails to state any federal offense jurisdictional?

sides.position: Cotton applies only where the indictment charges some federal crime but omits a necessary allegation; if the indictment fails to allege any federal offense at all, the defect remains jurisdictional and is not waivable.
cases: United States v. McIntosh, 704 F.3d 894 (11th Cir. 2013)

sides.position: Defects in an indictment, including failure to state an offense, are not jurisdictional under Cotton; the court has power to adjudicate the case regardless of the defect.
cases: United States v. De Vaughn, 694 F.3d 1141 (10th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Cothran, 302 F.3d 279 (5th Cir. 2002)
United States v. Muresanu, 951 F.3d 833 (7th Cir. 2020)

this_court: Adopts the Fifth and Tenth Circuit view that defects in an indictment are not jurisdictional, rejecting the Eleventh Circuit's narrower reading.
quote: The circuits are split on the proper interpretation of Cotton.
cite: United States v. Ionel Muresanu, 951 F.3d 833 (7th Cir. 2020)
